cycles.name: Uncoil
focuses: Restore the rotation the sport needs, hip and upper back, so the low back and forearm stop paying for what they cannot supply.
Get genuinely strong in the two patterns his tissues already own, supported knee-dominant and trunk-supported hinge, plus strapped pulling.
Gated on what a coach can actually see: filmed top sets and landings, a weekly symptom check-in, and a clinician on the wrist by 2026-08-22.

paragraphs: Your wrist hurts now. Before that it was your elbow. Same arm, same shot. I don't think that's bad luck.
When your hips and your upper back stop turning, something else has to turn instead. It ends up being your low back and your forearm. That's why this block starts by giving you your rotation back.
The other half is getting you properly strong. No back squat and no deadlift yet, you'll earn those next block. Don't read that as easy. The leg press is going to be heavy and I want it moving up.
Five weeks. Hips turning better, leg press up, and a quieter wrist without us really touching the wrist.
outcomes: Leg press and row both moving up, leg press by 10% or more
Wrist seen by a doctor or physio by the 22nd
Every top set filmed and sent
Landings clean enough to earn the box
Sitting longer before your back complains
Fewer forehands that bother the wrist

cycles.name: Brake Force
focuses: Eccentric and isometric braking capacity as the main strength stimulus, the highest-transfer quality the court demands and can never build.
Axial loading re-enters as the only new pattern of the cycle, and unilateral knee-dominant work begins.

paragraphs: Tennis is mostly stopping, and your court time can't build it because out there you never have to slow down more than your own bodyweight.
It's also the block where the bar comes back. You have to earn that with a clean five weeks here first.
Learn to stop and you get to everything else faster.

cycles.name: Chain Forge
focuses: Maximal strength, the longest and heaviest cycle, building the force ceiling everything later gets expressed against.
The free loaded hinge finally enters, alongside a genuine lean-mass dose and the first rotational throws.

cycles.name: Whipcrack
focuses: The serve and forehand chain, loaded and sequenced from the ground up through hip drive and trunk separation.
Overhead strength completes its ramp, plus explosive vertical and unilateral jumping.

cycles.name: Sidewinder
focuses: Multi-directional power and reactive change of direction, with lateral bounds entering here and nowhere earlier.
Frontal-plane hip, adductor and ankle control expressed under speed and under fatigue.

cycles.name: Third Set
focuses: Repeat power and pattern integrity under accumulated fatigue, the state tennis is actually played in.
Full re-test of the cycle 1 baseline battery and the written decision on where the next arc begins.

days.completionMessage: That's the heaviest work of your week finished. Get some carbs in you within the hour, you've earned them.

good: Steady, nose-breathing pace
Feel the legs warm through
bad: Don't race it, this is a raise not a session

good: Drive both knees to the floor
Feel the deep hip open at the back
bad: Don't let the ribs flare to fake the range

good: Turn your chest to the wall behind you
Feel it turn between the shoulder blades
bad: Don't let the low back do the turning

good: Push the floor away through the heels
Squeeze the glutes at the top
bad: Don't arch the low back to get higher

good: Pull the band to the walls
Feel the mid-back squeeze
bad: Don't shrug the shoulders up

exercises.name: Machine Leg Press
exercises.note: Stop the rep before your hips start rolling off the pad at the bottom. That tuck is your low back loading up in the exact position we're protecting, and it happens before you feel it. This is the lift I'm tracking all cycle, so film your heaviest set each week.

good: Push the platform away, feet flat
Feel the quads take the load through the whole rep
bad: Never let the hips roll off the pad at the bottom, stop the rep before the pelvis tucks

exercises.name: Machine Hip Thrust
exercises.note: Keep your ribs down and your chin tucked at the top. You're finishing this with your glutes, not by arching your back. Your hands stay off the load completely, that's your sore wrist.

good: Drive the pad to the ceiling through your heels
Feel the glutes finish the rep, not the low back
bad: Don't hyperextend at the top, ribs down and chin tucked

exercises.name: Chest-Supported Dumbbell Row
exercises.note: Use straps from day one. Your grip should never be the reason a set ends, not with your elbow and wrist history. This is the second lift I'm tracking, so push it.

good: Row the dumbbells to your hips
Feel the mid-back pull, not the arms
bad: Don't lift the chest off the pad to move more weight

exercises.name: Machine Chest Press
exercises.note: Neutral grip, and keep your wrist dead straight through the whole press. The moment it bends back under load it's your sore wrist taking it. Low volume here on purpose, you're a tennis player and you don't need much pressing.

good: Press the handles straight forward
Feel the chest do the work
bad: Don't let the wrist bend back under the load, keep it straight and neutral

exercises.name: Incline Y Raise
exercises.note: Rest your forehead on the pad and keep your eyes down the whole set. That keeps your neck completely neutral, which matters with your disc history. If there's no incline bench, do it standing against a wall with the back of your head touching.

good: Reach your thumbs to the top corners of the ceiling
Feel the muscle between the shoulder blades, low down
bad: Don't shrug, the shoulders stay down

good: Press straight out and hold the line
Feel the side of your trunk resist the pull
bad: Don't let your body twist toward the cable

days.completionMessage: Nobody sees this session and it's the one rebuilding the parts that kept breaking. Numbers logged, hips turning, feet getting stronger.

good: Easy steady pace
Just get warm
bad: Don't turn this into conditioning

good: Turn your elbow to the ceiling
Feel it turn between the shoulder blades
bad: Don't let the low back or hips move at all

good: Drive both knees to the floor
Feel the deep hip open at the back
bad: Don't let the ribs flare to fake the range

good: Drive the knee over the toes toward the wall
Feel the stretch behind the ankle
bad: Don't let the heel lift

good: Reach long, opposite arm and leg
Feel the low back stay flat on the floor
bad: Don't let the back arch off the floor

good: Pull your toes toward your shin
Feel the front of the shin
bad: Don't rock the body to help the toes up

exercises.name: Wrist Extension
exercises.note: This runs first, before anything else has tired the arm out. Same position and same weight every week so you can feel whether it's getting easier. It has to stay completely pain free, so if you feel anything at all, that's the end of it for that day and you tell me.

good: Hold the hand still against the resistance
Feel the forearm working, never the joint
bad: Stop immediately if it becomes sharp, this must stay completely pain free

exercises.name: Seated Banded Hip Internal Rotation
exercises.note: Stop at the first pinch you feel in the front of the hip. That pinch is your end range, it's not something to push through. This is the movement this whole block is built around, so don't rush it.

good: Turn the foot out and away against the band
Feel it deep in the back of the hip
bad: Stop at the first pinch in the front of the hip, that's your end range

exercises.name: Half-Kneeling Cable Thoracic Rotation
exercises.note: Your ribcage does the turning, not your hips and not your low back. If your belt buckle moves, you've stopped training the thing we're here for.

good: Turn your chest away from the machine
Feel the turn happen between the shoulder blades
bad: Don't let the low back or the hips turn, the ribcage does the work

good: Push the floor away through the big toe
Feel the calf lengthen slowly on the way down
bad: Don't bounce out of the bottom

exercises.name: Single-Leg Balance
exercises.note: Spread your toes and grip the floor. Don't let the arch collapse inward. Your flat feet are the bottom of every chain we're building above them, so this matters more than it looks.

good: Spread the toes and grip the floor
Feel the arch of the foot working to hold you
bad: Don't let the arch collapse inward

good: Make a double chin and hold
Feel the deep muscles at the front of the neck
bad: Don't tip the head back at any point

good: Push the floor away with the elbow
Feel the side of the trunk hold the line
bad: Don't let the hips sag toward the floor

days.completionMessage: Posterior chain and landings, both in the bank. That's the work that keeps your knee and your back out of trouble on court.

good: Push the ground away behind you
Feel the calves and glutes warm up
bad: Don't hold the handrails, walk it free

good: Drive both knees to the floor
Feel the deep hip open
bad: Don't flare the ribs to fake range

good: Reach the top arm to the floor behind you
Feel the chest and mid-back open
bad: Don't let the knees come apart

good: Push the floor away through the heels
Squeeze the glutes at the top
bad: Don't arch the low back

good: Pull the band to the walls
Feel the mid-back squeeze
bad: Don't shrug

exercises.name: Snap-Down
exercises.note: Weeks 1 and 2. No box, no height, just drop your hips fast and freeze. All we're building is a clean landing. If your knee falls inward at all, slow the drop right down until it doesn't.

good: Drop your hips fast and freeze like a statue
Feel the whole foot, knee and hip absorb it together
bad: Never let the knee fall inward, if it does slow the drop down

exercises.name: Box Drop
exercises.note: Weeks 3 to 5, and you don't get it by reaching week 3, you get it by earning it on film. Clean step downs and clean stick landings, both filmed and cleared by me, and no knee pain logged in weeks 1 and 2. Low box, and stop at 12 landings.

good: Land soft and freeze like a statue
Feel the whole foot, knee and hip absorb it together
bad: Never let the knee fall inward on landing, if it does lower the box

exercises.name: Dumbbell Reverse Lunge
exercises.note: Always step backward into it, never forward. Forward lunges load the knee in the position your ACL history doesn't want. Use straps if your grip gives out before your legs do.

good: Step back and sink straight down
Feel the front glute and quad take the weight
bad: Never step forward into it, always step back

exercises.name: 45° Back Extension
exercises.note: Your back doesn't move at all on this. If it rounds at the bottom or arches past straight at the top, that rep's over and your hips weren't doing the work. First two sessions, hold a dowel along your spine so head, mid back and hips all stay touching, and film one set.

good: Drive your hips into the pad to come up
Feel the glutes and hamstrings finish it
bad: Don't let your back move at all, if it rounds at the bottom or arches past straight at the top that rep is over

exercises.name: Machine Seated Leg Curl
exercises.note: This is the one that builds the muscle protecting your ACL knee when you land. Don't let your hips lift off the seat to finish a rep, that's your back taking over.

good: Curl the pad down toward your backside
Feel the back of the thigh do all of it
bad: Don't let your hips lift off the seat to finish the rep

exercises.name: Lat Pulldown
exercises.note: Straps on. Your grip is never the limiter here. Pull to your collarbone without leaning back and heaving it down.

good: Pull the bar to your collarbone
Feel the lats under the armpits
bad: Don't lean back and heave it down

exercises.name: Cable Face Pull
exercises.note: Keep your elbows at shoulder height or above the whole way. This one's for the back of your shoulders, which take a beating from serving and from swimming.

good: Pull the rope to your forehead and split it apart
Feel the back of the shoulders
bad: Don't let the elbows drop below the shoulders

good: Reach long through the fingertips and the heel
Feel the trunk stay completely still
bad: Don't let the hips rotate or the back arch

cards.title: Your pain rules
cards.body:
You've trained through pain before and it's the reason we're here. Your wrist, your elbow, your back, your knee. So let's make this simple. Telling me something hurts is not weakness and it never costs you your session.

Normal stuff you keep training through. Burning muscles, being tired, feeling stiff the next day. All fine.

Here's when you stop:

  • Mild and fading: finish the set, write it in your log.
  • Building through the set, or it changes how you move: stop that exercise, use the fallback on the card, message me.
  • Sharp, shooting, numb, pins and needles, or just new and weird: stop the session and message me before the next one.

Four extra rules for your history. Low back: anything going down your leg, stop right away. Neck: anything in your arm, pain or numbness or weakness, stop the session and stop serving, and see someone before the next one. Wrist: if the wrist hold hurts at all, it's done for that day. Knee: if your knee falls inward on a landing, the box goes lower.

cards.title: What happens when you tell me
cards.body:
I want you to read this now, before anything hurts, so you know exactly what reporting gets you. It gets you a change, not a ban.

  • Wrist worse: the cable rotation goes to a strap handle and the pulldown drops a set. Session still runs.
  • Back stiff: leg press drops a set and we tighten the depth. Session still runs.
  • Knee sore: box drops become step downs. Session still runs.

Notice the session always still runs. That's the whole point. Hiding it is the only thing that actually costs you training.

cards.title: How to find your weights
cards.body:
I don't put a weight on your card. You find it every session against the RPE number, and that number just means how hard the set should feel. RPE 8 means you finished with about two good reps still in you.

New movement: start lighter than you think. Do the first set, feel where the effort landed, then adjust. Being too light on set one costs you nothing.

Week to week: if you hit all your reps and it felt at or under the target, go up a small amount next time. If it was already at the top of the target, or you missed reps, stay on the same weight and do it again. Repeating a weight is not standing still.

Rough day: if a set is grinding harder than the number says it should, drop the weight. That's you reading it right, not you failing.

cards.title: Film these, every week
cards.body:
I'm not in the gym standing next to you, so video is how I actually coach you. Three things get filmed.

  • Leg press: your heaviest set, every week. I'm watching one thing, whether your hips stay on the pad at the bottom.
  • Back extension: one set in week 1 and one in week 2, with the dowel along your back so I can see it stays flat.
  • Step downs and stick landings: end of week 2. This is the film that decides whether you start box drops in week 3.

Send them to me on WhatsApp. Box drops don't start until I've seen that film and cleared it, and the leg press doesn't keep climbing if I can't see what your back is doing underneath it.

If the videos stop coming, the weight stops moving. Same deal I make with everyone.

cards.title: The wrist, honestly
cards.body:
Your wrist has been sore for a month and you're still hitting forehands on it every day. I'm not going to load it in the gym while that's true. But I also can't tell you what it is, and at fifteen there are a couple of things it could be that need a proper look, not a coach guessing.

Please get it checked by the 22nd. Take it to your physio or a doctor. Until then the only wrist work you do is that pain free hold, and it stays exactly where it is.

Go sooner if any of these turn up. Pain at night or when you're resting. It starting earlier in your sessions each week. Losing movement in the wrist. Pain over the bony part on the thumb side. Any numbness or pins and needles.

Here's the interesting bit. I think your wrist is a symptom, not the problem. If your hips and upper back start turning properly, your forearm stops having to do their job for them. Watch what happens to it over these five weeks.

cards.title: You need to eat more
cards.body:
You cut carbs to lose weight and take pressure off your joints. That made sense at the time. At fifteen, training this much, it's now working against you.

Your body is building bone and tendon right now and it can't do that on empty. A big chunk of the bone you'll carry as an adult gets laid down around your age. Miss that window and you don't get it back later.

So carbs come back in. Rice, bread, potatoes, fruit, around your training and your court sessions. Keep the protein where it is and add on top, don't swap one for the other.

I'm sending you to a nutritionist so this gets done properly instead of me guessing. Over the next few months your weight should be going up, not down.

cards.title: Your weekly check-in
cards.body:
Every rehab day starts with two minutes of this, before you touch anything else. No measuring, no equipment. I just need to know what your body is actually doing.

Four questions. Write the answers in your log:

  • How many minutes can you sit before your back starts talking to you?
  • Which side feels stiffer this week, left or right? Pick one, don't say neither.
  • How many forehands before the wrist starts? Give me a number.
  • Did anything stop you doing something this week, on court or in the gym?

You'll notice none of those can be answered with "I'm fine". That's on purpose.

Two other things. Weigh yourself every two weeks, morning, after the toilet, before you eat or drink. And once a month stand against a wall with a book flat on your head and measure it. You're fifteen and still growing, and that changes what I'll let you jump off.

If something hurts, tell me and I'll send you to someone who can properly look at it. My job is making you strong and keeping you moving. Working out what's going on inside a joint is a physio's job, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

cards.title: One full day off, every week
cards.body:
Right now your week is court five or six days, gym three days, plus swimming. Nobody has added that up, including you.

You get one full day a week with no court, no pool, no gym. Not the rehab day. A real one. This isn't me going soft on you, it's the day the work actually turns into strength.

Also tell me how much you're swimming. Sessions a week and roughly how long. Swimming is not recovery. It's a lot of shoulder and a lot of neck, and both of those are already on your list.

cards.title: You already did the hard part
cards.body:
Before we start, credit where it's due. Your back, your neck, your knee, your ankle, your elbow. You did the rehab on all of it and you stuck with it. That's the only reason we can train properly now instead of starting from zero.

Most people quit rehab halfway. You didn't.

The one thing still hanging around is the wrist, and it's the only one you never stopped and dealt with. Do the same thing with it that you did with the rest and you'll be in good shape.
